demo-bookstore-amazon-advertising-api-1:
Below is a quick‑start cheat‑sheet you can copy‑paste into your demo‑site docs.  
It gives you a **reasonable set of book‑categories** (you can start with these and later expand to the full BISAC list) and a **hand‑picked toolbox of public APIs** that complement the Amazon Product Advertising API (PA‑API).

---

## 1️⃣ Suggested Book Taxonomy (high‑level “menu” categories)

| Top‑Level Category | Typical Sub‑Categories (you can expose as dropdowns or facets) |
|--------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Fiction** | Literary, Mystery/Thriller, Romance, Science‑Fiction, Fantasy, Historical, Horror, LGBTQ+, Graphic Novels |
| **Non‑Fiction** | Biography & Memoir, History, Politics & Current Events, Business & Economics, Self‑Help, Health & Wellness, Travel, True Crime, Science & Nature, Philosophy, Religion & Spirituality |
| **Children & Middle‑Grade** | Picture Books, Early Readers, Chapter Books, Middle‑Grade (ages 8‑12) |
| **Young Adult (YA)** | YA Fantasy, YA Contemporary, YA Dystopia, YA Romance, YA Mystery |
| **Academic & Professional** | Textbooks (by discipline), Reference (Dictionaries, Encyclopedias), Test‑Prep, Technical (Engineering, Computer Science, Medicine), Law |
| **Special Interest** | Cookbooks, Arts & Photography, Sports & Outdoors, Music, Hobbies & Crafts, Parenting, Home & Garden |
| **Collections & Series** | Box Sets, Complete Series, Anthologies |
| **New Releases / Best‑Sellers** | “Just Arrived”, “Weekly Top 10”, “Amazon Choice”, “Award Winners” (Pulitzer, Booker, Hugo, etc.) |

> **Tip:** If you want a more exhaustive, industry‑standard list, adopt the **BISAC Subject Headings** (e.g., `FIC022000` = Science Fiction, `BIO001000` = Biography). You can store the code alongside the human‑readable label and map it to PA‑API’s `ItemAttributes/Subject` field.

---

## 2️⃣ Complementary APIs (beyond Amazon PA‑API)

| API | What It Gives You | Why It’s Useful for a Book Store Demo |
|-----|-------------------|---------------------------------------|
| **Google Books API** | Rich bibliographic metadata, preview snippets, cover thumbnails, ISBN lookup, language & page‑count info. | Quick fallback when Amazon data is missing; easy to embed a “Read a sample” preview. |
| **Open Library API** (Internet Archive) | Book details, cover images, author bios, edition history, OCLC numbers. | Free, open‑source data; great for older/out‑of‑print titles. |
| **ISBNdb API** | ISBN → title, author, publisher, publication date, dimensions, price ranges from multiple vendors. | Fast ISBN‑centric lookup; useful for bulk import or validation. |
| **Goodreads API** (read‑only; requires approval) | User ratings, reviews, shelves, author profiles, “What people are reading”. | Adds social proof (average rating, review count) to your product cards. |
| **LibraryThing API** | Tags, community reviews, “Similar books” recommendations. | Alternative social metadata; good for “Readers also liked” widgets. |
| **Book Depository API** (unofficial / partner) | International shipping prices, global availability. | Demonstrates cross‑border pricing & shipping options. |
| **Barnes & Noble Affiliate API** | Product details, pricing, availability for NB‑specific catalog. | Shows how you could aggregate multiple retailers. |
| **eBay Finding API** | Marketplace listings for used/rare books, price comparison. | Enables a “Used‑books” section or price‑match demo. |
| **Walmart Open API** (Books) | Pricing, inventory, reviews for Walmart’s book catalog. | Another retailer‑comparison data source. |
| **Amazon Marketplace Web Service (MWS)** | Order, inventory, and fulfillment data (if you ever go beyond a demo). | Useful if you later want to simulate real order processing. |
| **Amazon Advertising API** (formerly Product Advertising) | Sponsored product ads, keyword targeting, campaign reporting. | Shows how a store could monetize via Amazon ads. |
| **AWS Services (optional)** | S3 (store custom cover images), CloudFront (CDN), Cognito (auth), Lambda (serverless business logic), DynamoDB (catalog storage). | Gives you a full‑stack, cloud‑native demo environment. |

### Quick “stack” example for a demo

```text
Frontend (React / Vue) → API Gateway (Lambda) → 
   • Calls Amazon PA‑API for price/availability
   • Calls Google Books / Open Library for extra metadata
   • Calls Goodreads for rating & reviews
   • Stores custom images in S3 (served via CloudFront)
Auth → Amazon Cognito (optional)
```

---

## 3️⃣ How to Wire It Together (high‑level flow)

1. **User searches / browses a category** → UI sends a request to your backend (or directly to PA‑API if you expose the keys safely via a server‑side proxy).  
2. **Backend**  
   - Calls **PA‑API** with the search term / ASIN list → gets price, Amazon rating, buy‑button URL.  
   - Calls **Google Books** (or Open Library) with the same ISBN/ASIN → pulls description, author bio, preview link, cover image (fallback if Amazon image missing).  
   - Calls **Goodreads** (or LibraryThing) → fetches community rating & review count.  
   - Merges results into a single JSON payload (you can cache this in DynamoDB or Redis for demo speed).  
3. **Frontend** renders the product card:  
   - Cover image (Amazon → Google Books → Open Library fallback)  
   - Title, author, category badge (your taxonomy)  
   - Price & “Buy on Amazon” button (PA‑API)  
   - Community rating (Goodreads) + short excerpt (Google Books preview)  

---

## 4️⃣ Ready‑to‑Copy Sample Category JSON (BISAC style)

```json
{
  "categories": [
    {"code":"FIC000000","name":"Fiction"},
    {"code":"FIC001000","name":"Mystery & Detective"},
    {"code":"FIC002000","name":"Romance"},
    {"code":"FIC003000","name":"Science Fiction"},
    {"code":"FIC004000","name":"Fantasy"},
    {"code":"FIC005000","name":"Historical Fiction"},
    {"code":"FIC006000","name":"Horror"},
    {"code":"FIC007000","name":"Graphic Novels"},
    {"code":"BIO001000","name":"Biography & Autobiography"},
    {"code":"HIS001000","name":"History"},
    {"code":"BUS001000","name":"Business & Economics"},
    {"code":"SEL001000","name":"Self‑Help"},
    {"code":"HEA001000","name":"Health & Wellness"},
    {"code":"TRV001000","name":"Travel"},
    {"code":"COO001000","name":"Cookbooks"},
    {"code":"ART001000","name":"Arts & Photography"},
    {"code":"CHL001000","name":"Children’s Picture Books"},
    {"code":"CHL002000","name":"Early Readers"},
    {"code":"CHL003000","name":"Middle‑Grade"},
    {"code":"YAF001000","name":"Young Adult"},
    {"code":"EDU001000","name":"Academic & Textbooks"},
    {"code":"SPO001000","name":"Sports & Outdoors"},
    {"code":"MUS001000","name":"Music"},
    {"code":"HOM001000","name":"Home & Garden"}
  ]
}
```

You can load this at startup and use the `code` field for internal filtering while showing the `name` to shoppers.

---

## 5️⃣ One‑Liner Takeaway

- **Categories:** Start with a clean, shopper‑friendly hierarchy (Fiction, Non‑Fiction, Kids, YA, Academic, Special‑Interest, Collections, New/Best‑Sellers).  
- **APIs:** Pair **Amazon PA‑API** (price & buy‑button) with **Google Books** (metadata & preview) + **Open Library** (covers) + **Goodreads/LibraryThing** (ratings & reviews). Add **ISBNdb** for fast ISBN look‑ups and any retailer‑specific APIs (Barnes & Noble, Book Depository, eBay) if you want to showcase price‑comparison or affiliate‑link features.  

That’s all you need to spin up a realistic, data‑rich book‑store demo in a few hours. Happy coding! 🚀

**Japan in 14 Days – “First‑Timer’s Cultural‑History‑Nature Loop”**  
*(Tokyo → Hakone/Fuji → Kyoto/Osaka → Nara → Hiroshima → Miyajima → Nikko → Tokyo)*  

| Day | Region | Core Theme | Morning | Afternoon‑Evening | Overnight |
|-----|--------|------------|---------|-------------------|-----------|
| **1** | **Tokyo (Shinjuku)** | Arrival & orientation | Narita/Haneda → JR Yamanote to Shinjuku (≈30 min). Check‑in, freshen up. | Walk Shinjuku Gyoen (park + tea house). Dinner at Omoide Yokocho (yakitori). | Shinjuku |
| **2** | **Tokyo (Asakusa & Ueno)** | Old Edo | Senso‑ji temple, Nakamise‑shopping. | Ueno Park – Tokyo National Museum (samurai, ukiyo‑e). Evening stroll along Ameya‑Yokocho. | Asakusa |
| **3** | **Tokyo (Shibuya & Harajuku)** | Pop‑culture & tradition | Meiji Shrine (shinto ritual). | Harajuku Takeshita‑dori → Shibuya Crossing & Hachikō statue. Optional: Shibuya Sky observatory. | Shibuya |
| **4** | **Tokyo (Tsukiji & Ginza)** | Food & arts | Tsukiji Outer Market – sushi breakfast. | Ginza – Kabukiza Theatre (watch a 30‑min Kabuki act). Evening: river cruise on Sumida (night lights). | Ginza |
| **5** | **Hakone (Fuji‑area)** | Onsen & Mt Fuji | JR Tokaido Shinkansen to Odawara → Hakone Tozan Railway. Check‑in ryokan. | Hakone Ropeway → Owakudani (black‑egg tasting). Lake Ashi pirate‑ship cruise with Mt Fuji view. Onsen soak. | Hakone ryokan |
| **6** | **Hakone → Kyoto** | Transition | Early Hakone Open‑Air Museum (modern sculpture). | Return to Odawara → Shinkansen to Kyoto (≈2 h). Check‑in. Evening: Gion district walk, spot geisha. | Gion, Kyoto |
| **7** | **Kyoto (Eastern temples)** | Spiritual heritage | Kiyomizu‑dera (panoramic city view). | Walk the historic Higashiyama lane → Yasaka‑Shinjō (traditional shops). Tea ceremony at a machiya tea house (e.g., Camellia). | Kyoto |
| **8** | **Kyoto (Golden Pavilion & Arashiyama)** | Iconic sites & nature | Kinkaku‑ji (Golden Pavilion). | Arashiyama Bamboo Grove → Tenryū‑ji temple garden. Optional: boat on Hozu River. | Kyoto |
| **9** | **Osaka (Day‑trip)** | Food & nightlife | JR Kyoto → Osaka (15 min). Osaka Castle & park. | Dotonbori – takoyaki & okonomiyaki dinner. Nightlife in Namba. Return to Kyoto. | Kyoto |
| **10** | **Nara (Day‑trip)** | Ancient capital | JR Nara (45 min). Todai‑ji (Great Buddha) & Nara Park (deer feeding). | Kasuga‑Taisha shrine, traditional lanterns. Return to Kyoto. | Kyoto |
| **11** | **Hiroshima** | Peace & resilience | Shinkansen to Hiroshima (≈2 h). Check‑in. Visit Peace Memorial Park & Museum, A‑Bomb Dome. | Hiroshima‑style okonomiyaki for dinner. | Hiroshima |
| **12** | **Miyajima** | Sacred nature | Ferry to Itsukushima (≈30 min). Explore Itsukushima Shrine (floating torii). Hike or rope‑way to Mt Misen for panoramic sea view. | Return to Hiroshima. Optional night walk along the river. | Hiroshima |
| **13** | **Nikko** | UNESCO nature‑culture | Early Shinkansen to Utsunomiya → Tobu Nikko Line (≈2 h). Check‑in. Visit Toshogu Shrine (carved gold), Rinno‑ji, and the “see no evil” monkey bridge. | Walk around Lake Chuzenji & Kegon Falls (autumn colors if season). | Nikko |
| **14** | **Tokyo (Return)** | Last‑minute highlights | Tobu/Nikko → Tokyo (≈2 h). Quick stop at Akihabara for tech souvenirs or Yanaka‑Ginza for nostalgic streets. | Farewell dinner – izakaya in Roppongi or a kaiseki set in a ryokan‑style restaurant. Depart from Narita/Haneda (or stay one more night if flight is next day). | — |

---

## 1. Transportation Blueprint  

| Mode | Pass / Ticket | Coverage | Cost (approx.) | Tips |
|------|---------------|----------|----------------|------|
| **Japan Rail Pass** | 7‑day (¥29,650) or 14‑day (¥47,250) | Nationwide Shinkansen (except Nozomi), JR local lines, Miyajima ferry (JR) | Buy **before** arrival (online) → exchange at major airports. Activate on Day 5 (Hakone→Kyoto) to maximize usage. |
| **Regional Passes** | *Hakone Free Pass* (2‑day ¥4,600) – covers transport within Hakone, ropeway, pirate‑ship. | Use Day 5‑6. |
| **Local Metro/Subway** | Pre‑paid IC card (Suica/Pasmo) | Tokyo metro, buses, convenience‑store purchases. | Load ¥3,000; top‑up as needed. |
| **Ferries** | JR Miyajima Ferry (included in JR Pass) | Hiroshima ↔ Miyajima. |
| **Airport Transfers** | Narita Express (N’EX) – ¥3,000 (covered by JR Pass) or Keikyu Line (cheaper). | Use N’EX on Day 1. |
| **Luggage** | *Takuhaibin* (courier) | Ship large suitcases from Tokyo → Kyoto → Hiroshima → Tokyo to travel light on trains. | ~¥2,000 per bag, 1‑2 days. |

---

## 2. Accommodation Highlights  

| City | Neighborhood (Best for first‑timers) | Style | 2‑night average price (¥) |
|------|--------------------------------------|-------|---------------------------|
| **Tokyo – Shinjuku** | Shinjuku‑Kabukicho | Business hotel (e.g., **Hotel Gracery**) | 12,000 |
| **Tokyo – Asakusa** | Near Senso‑ji | Traditional ryokan‑style (e.g., **Asakusa View Hotel**) | 14,000 |
| **Hakone** | Near Lake Ashi | Onsen ryokan (e.g., **Yuryo Ryokan**) with private baths | 20,000‑30,000 |
| **Kyoto – Gion** | Gion/Higashiyama | Machiya townhouse (e.g., **Miyako Hotel**) | 15,000 |
| **Hiroshima** | Near Peace Park | Mid‑range hotel (e.g., **Sheraton Grand Hiroshima**) | 13,000 |
| **Nikko** | Nikko‑Onsen area | Ryokan with onsen (e.g., **Nikko Kanaya Hotel**) | 18,000 |

*All listed properties accept credit cards, have English staff, and provide free Wi‑Fi.*

---

## 3. Food & Dining – “Taste the Regions”

| Region | Must‑Try Dish | Recommended Spot (mid‑range) |
|--------|---------------|------------------------------|
| **Tokyo** | Sushi (early‑morning), Ramen (Tokyo‑style), Monjayaki (Tsukishima) | **Sushi Zanmai** (Tsukiji), **Ichiran** (Shibuya) |
| **Hakone** | Black‑egg (Owakudani), Kaiseki ryokan meals | **Gora Kadan** (kaiseki) |
| **Kyoto** | Yudofu (tofu hot‑pot), Kyo‑kaiseki, Matcha sweets | **Omen** (near Ginkaku‑ji), **Izuju** (Sannenzaka) |
| **Osaka** | Takoyaki, Okonomiyaki, Kushikatsu | **Mizuno** (Dotonbori), **Daruma** (Shinsekai) |
| **Nara** | Kakinoha‑zushi (persimmon‑leaf sushi), Nara‑style tea | **Kakinoha Sushi Hompo Tanaka** |
| **Hiroshima** | Hiroshima‑style okonomiyaki, Oysters | **Okonomimura** (multiple stalls) |
| **Miyajima** | Grilled oysters, Momiji‑man (maple‑leaf pastry) | **Miyajima Kaki‑ya** |
| **Nikko** | Yuba (tofu skin), Soba | **Hippari Dako** (near Toshogu) |

*Tip:* Reserve a **kaiseki** dinner in Kyoto (2‑course set) for a deep cultural immersion; many ryokans include it in the room rate.

---

## 4. Key Cultural Experiences (book in advance)

| Experience | Where | Approx. Cost (¥) | How to Book |
|------------|-------|-------------------|--------------|
| **Kimono rental & stroll** | Gion, Kyoto | 3,500‑5,000 (incl. photos) | Online via **Yumeyakata** or at rental shops on the day |
| **Tea ceremony** | Camellia (Kyoto) or Hamarikyu Gardens (Tokyo) | 4,000‑6,000 | Reserve 1‑2 weeks ahead |
| **Sumo practice viewing** | Arashio Beya (Tokyo) | 2,000 (donation) | Email the stable; limited slots |
| **Cooking class (Japanese home cooking)** | Osaka or Kyoto | 8,000‑12,000 | **AirKitchen** or **Voyagin** |
| **Nighttime lantern walk** | Nara Park (full moon) | Free | Check local event calendar (usually early Apr & Oct) |
| **Onsen private bath** | Hakone ryokan | Usually included in ryokan stay | Choose a ryokan with private onsen rooms |

---

## 5. Practical Tips for a Smooth Trip  

1. **Cash vs. Card** – Most restaurants accept cards, but small stalls, temples, and rural shops prefer cash. Carry a small amount of ¥2,000‑¥5,000 daily.  
2. **Language** – English signage is excellent on major stations and attractions; a translation app (Google Translate offline) helps in remote spots.  
3. **Seasonal Adjustments**  
   * **Spring (Mar‑May):** Add a day in **Kawaguchiko** for cherry‑blossom views of Mt Fuji.  
   * **Autumn (Oct‑Nov):** Keep the Nikko day (Lake Chuzenji & Kegon Falls) for peak foliage.  
   * **Winter (Dec‑Feb):** Swap Hakone for **Kusatsu Onsen** for snow‑capped Fuji views.  
4. **Etiquette Quick‑Guide** – Remove shoes when entering temples/ryokans, speak softly on trains, never tip, and line up orderly at food stalls.  
5. **Connectivity** – Rent a pocket Wi‑Fi (≈¥5,000/14 days) at the airport for navigation and translation.  
6. **Health** – Tap water is safe; carry a reusable bottle. Most onsen have separate male/female baths; modest swimwear is not allowed inside the baths.  

---

### Sample Day‑by‑Day Timeline (with travel times)

| Day | Travel | Time | Notes |
|-----|--------|------|-------|
| 1 | Airport → Shinjuku | 30 min (Narita Express) | Activate IC card. |
| 5 | Shinjuku → Odawara (Shinkansen) → Hakone Tozan | 1 h 30 min total | Use Hakone Free Pass for local rides. |
| 6 | Hakone → Odawara → Kyoto (Shinkansen) | 2 h | Activate JR Pass today. |
| 11 | Kyoto → Hiroshima (Shinkansen) | 2 h | Seat reservation (Green/Ordinary) via JR app. |
| 13 | Hiroshima → Tokyo → Nikko (Shinkansen + Tobu line) | 4 h total | Use JR Pass for Shinkansen; purchase Tobu Nikko Pass at Tokyo/Asakusa station. |

---

## 5. Quick‑Reference Checklist  

- **Passport & JR Pass voucher** (exchange at airport).  
- **IC Card (Suica/Pasmo)** + cash (¥5,000).  
- **Travel‑size Wi‑Fi router** (optional).  
- **Comfortable shoes** (lots of walking).  
- **Small day‑backpack** for snacks, water, umbrella.  
- **Portable charger** (train outlets are limited).  
- **Travel insurance** covering medical & luggage.  

---

### Bottom Line  

- **Cultural depth:** kimono, tea ceremony, sumo, cooking class, onsen.  
- **Historical weight:** Tokyo’s shrines, Kyoto’s UNESCO temples, Nara’s ancient capital, Hiroshima’s Peace Park, Himeji Castle (optional add‑on if you have an extra day).  
- **Nature balance:** Hakone’s lake & hot springs, Arashiyama bamboo, Miyajima’s sea‑mountain, Nikko’s waterfalls, optional day‑trip to the Japanese Alps (if you swap Osaka for Takayama).  

Follow the table above, book the few experiences a week ahead, and you’ll return home with a **well‑rounded portrait of Japan’s past, present, and natural soul**—all without feeling rushed. Safe travels!

We expand the right end of the window one character at a time. If the new character is already in the window, we shrink the left end until the duplicate is removed. Throughout the process we keep the maximum window size seen.

**2. Code (Python)**  
```python
def length_of_longest_substring(s: str) -> int:
    """
    Returns the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
    """
    char_index = {}          # maps character -> its latest index
    left = 0                 # left boundary of the sliding window
    max_len = 0

    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        # If ch was seen and lies inside the current window, move left
        if ch in char_index and char_index[ch] >= left:
            left = char_index[ch] + 1
        char_index[ch] = right
        max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)

    return max_len
```

**3. Complexity analysis**  
- **Time:** `O(n)` – each character is visited at most twice (once by `right`, once by moving `left`).  
- **Space:** `O(min(m, n))` – at most one entry per distinct character (`m` = size of the character set, `n` = length of `s`).

**4. Example test cases**  

| Input                | Output |
|----------------------|--------|
| `"abcabcbb"`         | `3`    |
| `"bbbbb"`            | `1`    |
| `"pwwkew"`           | `3`    |
| `""` (empty string) | `0`    |
| `"au"`               | `2`    |

**5. Edge Cases**  
- Empty string → return `0`.  
- All characters identical → return `1`.  
- String containing Unicode characters → works unchanged (Python’s `dict` handles Unicode).

**7. Additional notes**  
The algorithm updates `left` only when a duplicate is found inside the current window, ensuring linear time.

A linear‑time sliding‑window algorithm efficiently finds the longest substring without repeated characters.

jobs-search-and-salary-research-1:
**Solution Explanation**

For a string `S` we have to find the longest substring `T`

* `T` is a prefix of `S`
* `T` is a suffix of `S`
* `T` occurs somewhere else inside `S` (i.e. not only as the prefix and the suffix)

If no such substring exists we have to output  

```
Just a legend
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 1.   Prefix function  

For every position `i` (`0 … n‑1`)  

```
π[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of S[0…i]
       which is also a suffix of S[0…i]
```

`π` can be built in `O(n)` (the classic KMP preprocessing).

*If a string is a prefix and a suffix of the whole word, its length is a
border of the whole word – exactly a value `π[n‑1]` or one of its
ancestors (`π[π[n‑1]‑1]`, `π[π[π[n‑1]‑1]‑1]`, …).*

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 2.   When does a border appear in the middle?

Assume a length `L` is a border of the whole string (`L = π[n‑1]` or a
smaller border).  
`L` also occurs somewhere inside the word **iff** there is an index
`i < n‑1` with `π[i] ≥ L`.  
Indeed `π[i] ≥ L` means that the prefix of length `L` is a suffix of the
prefix `S[0…i]`, i.e. it appears ending at position `i` – a middle
occurrence.

So we need the **largest** border `L` such that  

```
max_{0 ≤ i < n‑1} π[i]  ≥  L
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 3.   Algorithm  

```
build π[0…n‑1]
mx = max{ π[i] | 0 ≤ i < n‑1 }          // longest border that appears before the end
L  = π[n‑1]                            // longest border of the whole string

while L > 0
        if mx ≥ L          answer = S[0…L‑1]   // found the required substring
        else               L = π[L‑1]        // try the next shorter border
output "Just a legend" if L became 0
```

The loop follows the chain of borders (`π[L‑1]` is the next shorter border)
and stops at the first one that also occurs in the middle.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 4.   Correctness Proof  

We prove that the algorithm prints exactly the required substring or
states correctly that none exists.

---

##### Lemma 1  
For any length `L` that is a border of `S` (i.e. `L = π[n‑1]` or a
descendant of it) there exists a middle occurrence of the prefix of
length `L` **iff** `mx ≥ L`.

**Proof.**  
`mx` is the maximum value of `π[i]` for `i < n‑1`.  
*If* `mx ≥ L`, then there is an index `i < n‑1` with `π[i] ≥ L`. By the
definition of `π[i]` the prefix of length `L` is a suffix of
`S[0…i]`, therefore it occurs ending at `i` – a middle occurrence.

*Conversely*, if the prefix of length `L` occurs somewhere inside `S`,
let that occurrence end at position `i` (`i < n‑1`). Then `π[i] ≥ L`,
hence `mx ≥ L`. ∎



##### Lemma 2  
During the loop the variable `L` always holds a border length of `S`.

**Proof.**  
Initially `L = π[n‑1]`, a border of the whole string.  
If the current `L` is not suitable we set `L = π[L‑1]`.  
`π[L‑1]` is the longest proper border of the prefix of length `L`,
therefore it is a shorter border of the whole string. By induction the
property holds for every iteration. ∎



##### Lemma 3  
If the algorithm outputs a string `T`, then `T` satisfies all three
requirements.

**Proof.**  
`T` is `S[0…L‑1]` for the first `L` that makes the condition
`mx ≥ L` true.

* Prefix – by construction `T` is a prefix.
* Suffix – because `L` is a border (Lemma 2), `T` is also a suffix.
* Middle occurrence – `mx ≥ L` holds, therefore by Lemma 1 the
  prefix of length `L` appears somewhere before the last character,
  i.e. in the middle.

Thus `T` fulfills all conditions. ∎



##### Lemma 4  
If a suitable substring exists, the algorithm will output one.

**Proof.**  
Let `L*` be the **longest** length that satisfies the three conditions.
`L*` is a border, so it appears in the chain
`π[n‑1] , π[π[n‑1]‑1] , …`.  
All longer borders are examined earlier in the loop. For each of them
`mx < L` (otherwise they would be a longer suitable length, contradicting
maximality of `L*`).  
When the loop reaches `L = L*`, we have `mx ≥ L*` (Lemma 1), the
condition becomes true and the algorithm outputs the substring of length
`L*`. ∎



##### Lemma 5  
If the algorithm prints “Just a legend”, no suitable substring exists.

**Proof.**  
The algorithm prints this text only after the loop reduces `L` to `0`,
i.e. every border length `L > 0` has been examined and for each of them
`mx < L`. By Lemma 1 none of those borders occurs in the middle,
hence no substring can satisfy all three requirements. ∎



##### Theorem  
The algorithm always prints the longest substring that is simultaneously
a prefix, a suffix and occurs elsewhere inside the given string; if no
such substring exists it prints “Just a legend”.

**Proof.**  
*Existence case*: By Lemma 4 the algorithm outputs a substring.
Lemma 3 guarantees that this substring satisfies the requirements.
Because the loop checks borders from longest to shortest, the first
found one is the longest possible.

*Non‑existence case*: By Lemma 5 the algorithm prints
“Just a legend” only when no suitable substring exists.

Thus the output is correct in all cases. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 5.   Complexity Analysis  

*Building the prefix function* – `O(n)` time, `O(n)` memory.  
*Scanning for `mx`* – `O(n)` time.  
*Loop over borders* – each step shortens `L`, at most `O(n)` steps,
overall `O(n)` time.

Total: **`O(n)` time**, **`O(n)` additional memory** (`π` array).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 6.   Reference Implementation  (GNU‑C++17)

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    
    string s;
    if (!(cin >> s)) return 0;
    int n = (int)s.size();

    // 1. prefix function
    vector<int> pi(n, 0);
    for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
        int j = pi[i - 1];
        while (j > 0 && s[i] != s[j]) j = pi[j - 1];
        if (s[i] == s[j]) ++j;
        pi[i] = j;
    }

    // 2. longest border that appears before the last character
    int mx = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; ++i) mx = max(mx, pi[i]);

    // 3. walk through the chain of borders
    int L = pi[n - 1];                 // longest border of the whole string
    while (L > 0) {
        if (mx >= L) {                 // middle occurrence exists
            cout << s.substr(0, L) << '\n';
            return 0;
        }
        L = pi[L - 1];                 // next shorter border
    }

    cout << "Just a legend\n";
    return 0;
}
```

The program follows exactly the algorithm proven correct above and
conforms to the GNU++17 compiler.

To support these capabilities we should look for APIs that:

1. **Handle geographic queries** – converting addresses to coordinates and vice‑versa, and calculating distances.  
2. **Provide nearby transit or routing information** – to determine how close a property is to metro stations or other transport hubs.  
3. **Offer location‑based search** – returning places that match a proximity filter.  

Scanning the available APIs, the ones that deal with geocoding, routing, local search and geographic utilities are the best fit. No API is explicitly about real‑estate listings, so we focus on the geographic and proximity‑search capabilities.

Below is a compact, production‑ready recipe for the **OAuth 1.0a “three‑legged” flow** with Twitter, using the `requests_oauthlib` library in Python. After the flow you’ll have a user‑specific `oauth_token` and `oauth_token_secret` that you can store and reuse for any Twitter API endpoint (e.g. fetching a timeline). The example also shows how to handle the most common error conditions, rate‑limit handling, and pagination. --- ## 1️⃣ Prerequisites ```bash pip install requests requests_oauthlib ``` * **Consumer (API) key** → `API_KEY` * **Consumer secret** → `API_SECRET` * **Callback URL** (must be registered in the Twitter dev portal) → e.g. `https://your‑domain.com/callback` --- ## 2️⃣ Minimal Flask app for the OAuth callback ```python # app.py from flask import Flask, request, redirect, session, url_for, render_template_string from requests_oauthlib import OAuth1Session import os, json, time app = Flask(__name__) app.secret_key = os.getenv('FLASK_SECRET', 'dev‑secret') # keep this safe! # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- # 1️⃣ Obtain a request token # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- REQUEST_TOKEN_URL = 'https://api.twitter.com/oauth/request_token' AUTHORIZATION_URL = 'https://api.twitter.com/oauth/authorize' ACCESS_TOKEN_URL = 'https://api.twitter.com/oauth/access_token' CONSUMER_KEY = os.getenv('TWITTER_API_KEY') CONSUMER_SECRET = os.getenv('TWITTER_API_SECRET') @app.route('/') def index(): """Start the OAuth flow – redirect user to Twitter.""" oauth = OAuth1Session(CONSUMER_KEY, client_secret=CONSUMER_SECRET, callback_uri=url_for('callback', _external=True)) try: fetch_response = oauth.fetch_request_token(REQUEST_TOKEN_URL) except Exception as e: return f'Error obtaining request token: {e}', 500 # Store request token secret in the session (or DB) for later use session['resource_owner_key'] = fetch_response.get('oauth_token') session['resource_owner_secret'] = fetch_response.get('oauth_token_secret') # Build the URL the user must visit to authorize the app authorization_url = oauth.authorization_url(AUTHORIZATION_URL) return redirect(authorization_url) # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- # 2️⃣ Callback – exchange verifier for an access token # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- @app.route('/callback') def callback(): """Twitter redirects here after the user authorizes.""" oauth_token = request.args.get('oauth_token') oauth_verifier = request.args.get('oauth_verifier') # Retrieve the request token secret we saved earlier resource_owner_key = session.get('resource_owner_key') resource_owner_secret = session.get('resource_owner_secret') if not (resource_owner_key and resource_owner_secret): return 'Missing request token in session', 400 oauth = OAuth1Session(CONSUMER_KEY, client_secret=CONSUMER_SECRET, resource_owner_key=resource_owner_key, resource_owner_secret=resource_owner_secret, verifier=oauth_verifier) try: oauth_tokens = oauth.fetch_access_token(ACCESS_TOKEN_URL) except Exception as e: return f'Error fetching access token: {e}', 500 # Store the user‑specific tokens securely (DB, encrypted file, vault, …) user_access_token = oauth_tokens.get('oauth_token') user_access_secret = oauth_tokens.get('oauth_token_secret') screen_name = oauth_tokens.get('screen_name') user_id = oauth_tokens.get('user_id') # For demo purposes we just keep them in the session session['access_token'] = user_access_token session['access_secret'] = user_access_secret session['screen_name'] = screen_name session['user_id'] = user_id return redirect(url_for('timeline')) # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- # 3️⃣ Use the access token to call a protected endpoint (e.g. user timeline) # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- @app.route('/timeline') def timeline(): """Fetch and display the authenticated user's timeline.""" access_token = session.get('access_token') access_secret = session.get('access_secret') if not (access_token and access_secret): return redirect(url_for('index')) oauth = OAuth1Session(CONSUMER_KEY, client_secret=CONSUMER_SECRET, resource_owner_key=access_token, resource_owner_secret=access_secret) # 'max_id': , # for next page (see pagination section) 'tweet_mode': 'extended' # get full text } try: resp = oauth.get(timeline_url, params=params, timeout=10) except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e: return f'Network error: {e}', 502 # Get request token** | `oauth.fetch_request_token(REQUEST_TOKEN_URL)` | Signed with consumer key/secret; Twitter returns `oauth_token` & `oauth_token_secret`. | | **B. Redirect user** | `redirect(oauth.authorization_url(AUTHORIZATION_URL))` | Sends the user to Twitter’s authorize page. | | **C. Receive verifier** | `request.args.get('oauth_verifier')` (in `/callback`) | Twitter redirects back with `oauth_token` and `oauth_verifier`. | | **D. Exchange for access token** | `oauth.fetch_access_token(ACCESS_TOKEN_URL)` | Returns `oauth_token` (user’s access token) and `oauth_token_secret`. | | **E. Store tokens** | Save `access_token` & `access_secret` (session, DB, vault) | Needed for all subsequent API calls. | | **F. Signed API request** | `OAuth1Session(...).get(endpoint, params=…)` | The library automatically adds the OAuth `Authorization` header. | | **G. Parse JSON** | `resp.json()` | Gives you native Python structures. | | **H. Rate‑limit handling** | Check `resp.headers['x-rate-limit-remaining']` and `x-rate-limit-reset` | If `remaining == 0` or you get 429, sleep until reset. | | **I. Pagination** | Use `max_id` (older) or `since_id` (newer) query parameters | Loop until no new `max_id` is returned. | | **J. Error handling** | `try/except` around `requests` + status‑code checks | 401 → token revoked/invalid, 429 → rate limit, other 4xx/5xx → network or API errors. | --- ## 3️⃣ Common “what‑if” scenarios | Situation | Detection | Recommended response | |-----------|-----------|----------------------| | **User revokes app** | API returns **401 Unauthorized** with `error` “Invalid or expired token” | Clear stored tokens, redirect user through the auth flow again. | | **App deleted from developer portal** | Same 401 response (or 403) | Treat as revoked – ask the user to reinstall or contact you. | | **User changes password / email** | Tokens remain valid (OAuth 1.0a tokens are not tied to password) – no action needed. | | **Rate limit exceeded** | HTTP **429** + `x-rate-limit-reset` header | Sleep until the reset timestamp (or back‑off exponentially). | | **Network glitch** | `requests.exceptions.*` | Retry with exponential back‑off (max 3‑5 attempts). | | **Invalid request parameters** | 4xx other than 401/429 (e.g., 400 Bad Request) | Log the error, surface a friendly message to the user. | | **Pagination needed** | `max_id`/`since_id` in response or `next_cursor` for collections | Loop: request next page until the cursor is `0` or `None`. | **Sample pagination loop (user timeline):** ```python def fetch_all_tweets(oauth, screen_name, max_pages=5): url = 'https://api.twitter.com/1.1/statuses/user_timeline.json' params = {'screen_name': screen_name, 'count': 200, 'tweet_mode': 'extended'} all_tweets = [] max_id = None for _ in range(max_pages): if max_id: params['max_id'] = max_id resp = oauth.get(url, params=params) if resp.status_code != 200: raise RuntimeError(f'API error {resp.status_code}: {resp.text}') batch = resp.json() if not batch: break all_tweets.extend(batch) max_id = batch[-1]['id'] - 1 # next page older than last tweet return all_tweets ``` --- ## 4️⃣ Optional: Use **Tweepy** for a higher‑level wrapper If you prefer not to hand‑craft every request, Tweepy already implements the OAuth 1.0a flow and provides helpers for pagination, rate‑limit handling, and error classes. ```bash pip install tweepy ``` ```python import tweepy, os, flask app = flask.Flask(__name__) auth = tweepy.OAuth1UserHandler( consumer_key=os.getenv('TWITTER_API_KEY'), consumer_secret=os.getenv('TWITTER_API_SECRET'), callback='https://your-domain.com/callback' ) @app.route('/') def login(): try: redirect_url = auth.get_authorization_url() flask.session['request_token'] = auth.request_token return flask.redirect(redirect_url) except tweepy.TweepError as e: return f'Auth error: {e}', 500 @app.route('/callback') def callback(): verifier = flask.request.args.get('oauth_verifier') token = flask.session.pop('request_token') auth.request_token = token try: auth.get_access_token(verifier) except tweepy.TweepError as e: return f'Access token error: {e}', 500 api = tweepy.API(auth) tweets = api.user_timeline(screen_name=auth.get_username(), count=20, tweet_mode='extended') return '

It was a rain‑slick night in the city, the kind that makes the neon flicker like a dying heartbeat. I was nursing a glass of bourbon in my office when the dame walked in—tall, red‑lipped, and clutching a leather‑bound ledger that had gone missing from the mayor’s vault.

“Mr. Archer,” she whispered, “they say the ledger holds the names of every contract the mayor’s been shaking down. If it falls into the wrong hands… the whole city will burn.”

She slid the empty file across my desk. No fingerprints, no prints, just a thin smear of oil. The usual suspects—corrupt officials, street thugs—were all dead ends. I needed something more… precise.

I turned on the old Q‑Box, a quantum computer I’d salvaged from a defunct research lab. Its cryogenic coils hummed, and the qubits settled into a fragile superposition. I fed the Q‑Box the ledger’s last known hash, the oil’s chemical signature, and the city’s surveillance feeds. Using Grover’s algorithm, the machine could search the million‑plus possible locations in a fraction of the time a human could.

The middle of the case unfolded in a blur of entangled data. The Q‑Box projected a probability map onto the wall—bright spots where the ledger might be, dimmer where it wasn’t. One node glowed like a beacon: the abandoned warehouse on Dockside, a place the mayor’s men used for “off‑the‑books” meetings.

I grabbed my coat, the dame’s warning echoing in my ears, and headed for the dock. The rain hammered the metal doors as I forced them open. Inside, the ledger lay on a rusted table, surrounded by a circle of men in dark suits. Their eyes widened when they saw me; they hadn’t expected a private eye with a quantum computer in his pocket.

I pulled the Q‑Box from my coat, its screen flashing the decrypted ledger. The quantum processor had not only located the file but also cracked the encryption on the mayor’s private communications, exposing a network of bribery and murder. The men tried to flee, but the police—alerted by the dame’s call—stormed in and cuffed them.

The end came with the ledger safely back in the mayor’s hands, the city’s secrets exposed, and the dame’s gratitude as fleeting as the rain. I tipped my hat, poured another bourbon, and watched the Q‑Box cool down. In a world of shadows and lies, sometimes the only way to see the truth is to let a few qubits dance in the dark.

- ✅ Persona sketch completed  
- ✅ Voice & tone defined  
- ✅ Deadline entered in calendar  

---

## 🔎 2. Keyword & Search‑Intent Research  

1. **Primary keyword** – the exact phrase you want to rank for.  
   - Example: **“benefits of professional cleaning service”**  

2. **LSI (Latent Semantic Indexing) keywords** – synonyms & related terms that Google expects in a comprehensive article.  
   - Examples: “advantages of hiring a cleaning company,” “why use a cleaning service,” “professional cleaning vs DIY,” “home cleaning benefits,” “commercial cleaning ROI.”

## 📄 3. Draft a Detailed Content Brief

| **Cronofy** | Calendar (Google, Outlook, iCloud, Exchange, Office 365) + Scheduling UI | `https://api.cronofy.com/v1/` | OAuth 2.0 per provider | Great if you need a single calendar abstraction. |
| **Zapier / Make (Integromat)** | “Glue” layer – triggers & actions across > 3 000 apps | N/A (webhooks) | API Key / OAuth | Use for rapid prototyping or fallback when a native API is missing. |

---

## 📦 How to Wire It All Together (High‑Level Architecture)

1. **OAuth 2.0 Provider Manager**  
   - Centralize token acquisition/refresh for each vendor (Google, Microsoft, Slack, etc.).  
   - Store tokens securely (encrypted at rest, use a vault like AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault).  

2. **Domain‑Specific Service Clients**  
   - Write thin wrapper classes (`GmailClient`, `GraphMailClient`, `SlackClient`, …) that expose a **common interface** (e.g., `sendMessage(to, subject, body)`).  
   - Use a **factory** that picks the right implementation based on the user’s linked accounts.

3. **Unified Data Model**  
   - Define internal POJOs / Pydantic models: `Email`, `Event`, `Contact`, `Task`, `Note`, `Message`, `File`.  
   - Map each provider’s JSON payload to these models (adapter pattern).  

4. **Orchestration Layer**  
   - A **command‑handler** (e.g., `CreateMeetingCommand`) that can:  
     1. Pull participants from contacts.  
     2. Check free/busy via Calendar APIs.  
     3. Create an event (Google Calendar **or** Graph).  
     4. Send invites via Mail API.  
     5. Add a note to OneNote/Evernote.  
   - Use a **workflow engine** (Temporal, Cadence, or simple async task queue) for long‑running actions.

5. **Security & Compliance**  
   - Scope‑least‑privilege: request only the OAuth scopes you need (`mail.read`, `mail.send`, `calendar.events`, `contacts.read`, `files.readwrite`).  
   - Implement **token revocation** UI so users can disconnect a provider at any time.  
   - Log audit events (who accessed which service, when).  

6. **Rate‑Limit & Retry Strategy**  
   - Respect each provider’s `X‑RateLimit‑*` headers.  
   - Exponential back‑off with jitter (e.g., `retry-after` or 429 → wait 2ⁿ seconds).  
   - Cache immutable data (e.g., contact list) for a short TTL to reduce calls.

7. **Testing & Mocking**  
   - Use the official sandbox environments (Google’s “OAuth Playground”, Microsoft Graph “sandbox”, Slack “development workspace”).  
   - For CI, mock with libraries like `responses` (Python) or `nock` (Node) and store sample JSON fixtures.

---

## 🎯 Quick “Starter” Stack (example)

| Layer | Tech | Why |
|-------|------|-----|
| **Auth** | `authlib` (Python) / `passport‑azure‑ad` (Node) | Full OAuth 2.0 + PKCE support. |
| **HTTP** | `httpx` (Python) / `axios` (Node) | Async, auto‑retry, easy to plug interceptors for rate‑limit handling. |
| **Data Models** | Pydantic (Python) / TypeScript interfaces | Validation + automatic JSON ↔ object conversion. |
| **Task Queue** | **Celery** (Python) + Redis **or** **BullMQ** (Node) | Background jobs for sending emails, uploading files, etc. |
| **Workflow** | **Temporal.io** (language‑agnostic) | Guarantees exactly‑once execution for multi‑step commands. |
| **Storage** | PostgreSQL (JSONB for raw payloads) + Redis (cache) | Relational for user accounts, flexible for provider‑specific blobs. |
| **Secrets** | AWS Secrets Manager / HashiCorp Vault | Secure token storage, automatic rotation. |
| **Observability** | OpenTelemetry + Grafana Loki | Trace cross‑service calls (Google → Graph → Slack). |

The rain hammered the neon‑slick streets of New Harbor like a jittery metronome, and I was standing under the flickering sign of the Olde Lantern Bar, nursing a glass of cheap bourbon that tasted like regret. I’d been a gumshoe for thirty‑odd years, a veteran of every crooked alley and back‑room deal the city could conjure. The badge I’d once worn was now a rusted relic in a drawer, but the instincts never left.

She walked in like a cold draft—silk coat, eyes the color of midnight oil, a smile that could melt steel. “Detective Marlowe,” she whispered, sliding a manila envelope across the bar. “My husband’s gone missing. All that’s left is this.” She tapped the side of the envelope, and a faint blue glow pulsed from within.

Inside was a sleek, black slab no bigger than a briefcase, its surface etched with a lattice of glowing lines. The label read: **Q‑Box 1.0 – Quantum Computational Core**. In a city where the only computers were clunky mainframes that coughed out numbers like a dying horse, this thing looked like something out of a science‑fiction fever dream.

“Your husband was a physicist,” I said, eyes narrowing. “What does a quantum computer have to do with a disappearance?”

She hesitated, then whispered, “He was working on a project—something called ‘Entangled Echo.’ He said it could predict events before they happened. Then he vanished. The Q‑Box is the only thing left.”

I took the slab to my office, a cramped attic above a laundromat that smelled of detergent and stale cigarettes. The Q‑Box hummed, its quantum bits dancing in a state of superposition, a ghostly chorus of possibilities. I fed it the data: the husband’s research notes, the last known location, the timeline of the night he disappeared.

The machine whirred, its qubits entangling with the information, collapsing into a single, stark answer: **“Subterranean Lab, 23rd Street, 02:17 AM – Security Override: 0x7F3A.”** The quantum computer had sliced through the noise of the city’s chaos and pinpointed a hidden facility beneath the old textile mill.

I grabbed my coat, my revolver, and a battered notebook, and headed out into the storm. The mill loomed like a rusted beast, its windows blackened. I slipped through a service door, descended a rusted stairwell, and found a door marked **“Project Entangled Echo.”** Inside, a lab of humming servers and a lone figure slumped over a console—Dr. Alden Voss, the missing husband, eyes glazed, his mind frayed by the very quantum predictions he’d chased.

He looked up, a flicker of recognition in his eyes. “You used the Q‑Box,” he rasped. “It showed me the future… and the future showed me my own death.”

I cuffed him, the rain still pounding the city outside, and the Q‑Box sat silent on the table, its power both a blessing and a curse. In a world where shadows and photons collided, I’d learned that even a seasoned detective could trust a quantum ghost to illuminate the darkest mysteries.

The classic, portable way on any Unix‑like system is to let **`find`** walk the tree for you.  
It handles every possible filename (including spaces, new‑lines, Unicode, etc.) and lets you filter or act on the results in one go.

```bash
# All regular files under /some/dir (including sub‑dirs)
find /some/dir -type f

# If you only want the names, one per line (the default)
find . -type f

# Safer for weird filenames – NUL‑separated output
find . -type f -print0 | xargs -0 <command‑or‑process>

# Example: feed the list to another program
find . -type f -print0 | xargs -0 md5sum
```

### Why `find` is usually the “best” choice

| Feature | `find` | `ls -R` | `tree` |
|---------|--------|----------|--------|
| Recurses into sub‑directories automatically | ✅ | ✅ (but output is meant for human eyes) | ✅ |
| Handles any filename (spaces, new‑lines, control chars) | ✅ (`-print0` + `xargs -0`) | ❌ (`ls` splits on whitespace) | ✅ (with `-0`) |
| Easy to filter (by name, size, mtime, permissions, etc.) | ✅ (`-name`, `-size`, `-mtime`, …) | ❌ | ✅ (limited) |
| No extra packages required (coreutils) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ (needs `tree` package) |
| Can execute a command on each file (`-exec`, `-execdir`, `+`) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Fast for huge trees (no extra formatting) | ✅ | ❌ (lots of extra output) | ✅ (but adds overhead) |

### Common variations

* **Only regular files** – `-type f` (as shown above).  
* **Only directories** – `-type d`.  
* **Exclude hidden files** – `find . -type f ! -name '.*'`.  
* **Limit depth** – `-maxdepth N` (e.g., `-maxdepth 2`).  
* **Print full path** – default; use `-printf '%p\n'` for custom formatting.  
* **List with details** – `find . -type f -exec ls -l {} +`.  

### Alternatives (when you really need them)

* **`tree`** – nice pretty‑printed tree, and with `-if --noreport` it can output a plain list of files.  
  ```bash
  tree -if --noreport /some/dir
  ```
* **`ls -R`** – recursive `ls`, but its output is meant for humans and breaks on odd filenames; not recommended for scripting.

In practice, for any script or command line where you just need “all the files under this directory (recursively)”, `find` is the most robust, flexible, and universally available tool.

coindesk-guardian-news-1:
**How to Summarize Text with the OpenAI API**

---

### 1️⃣ Quick Overview
The OpenAI API lets you send a piece of text to a language model (e.g., `gpt‑3.5‑turbo` or `gpt‑4`) and receive a concise summary in return.  
Think of it as asking a very smart assistant: *“Can you give me the main points of this article?”*

---

### 2️⃣ Step‑by‑Step Guide

| Step | What to Do | Why It Matters |
|------|------------|----------------|
| **1. Get an API key** | Sign up at [platform.openai.com](https://platform.openai.com) → **API Keys** → **Create new key**. | Authenticates your requests. |
| **2. Install the client** | ```bash pip install openai``` | Provides a convenient wrapper for HTTP calls. |
| **3. Choose a model** | `gpt-3.5-turbo` (fast & cheap) or `gpt-4` (higher quality). | Determines cost, speed, and output quality. |
| **4. Write a prompt** | Use a clear instruction, e.g., `"Summarize the following text in 3‑5 sentences:"`. | Good prompts give reliable summaries. |
| **5. Call the API** | Send a **chat** or **completion** request with your text. | The model processes the prompt + text. |
| **6. Extract the summary** | Read `response.choices[0].message.content` (chat) or `response.choices[0].text` (completion). | This is the final summarized output. |

---

### 3️⃣ Minimal Python Example (Chat Completion)

```python
import openai

# 1️⃣ Set your secret key
openai.api_key = "sk-YOUR_API_KEY"

# 2️⃣ The text you want summarized
long_text = """
Artificial intelligence (AI) is a field of computer science that aims to create machines
capable of intelligent behavior. ... (more paragraphs) ...
"""

# 3️⃣ Build the request
response = openai.ChatCompletion.create(
    model="gpt-3.5-turbo",          # or "gpt-4"
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user",
         "content": f"Summarize the following text in 3‑5 sentences:\n\n{long_text}"}
    ],
    temperature=0.3,                # lower = more deterministic
    max_tokens=150                  # limit length of the summary
)

# 4️⃣ Print the summary
summary = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
print("📝 Summary:\n", summary)
```

**Result (example)**  
```
📝 Summary:
Artificial intelligence (AI) studies how to build machines that can perform tasks requiring human-like intelligence. It encompasses subfields such as machine learning, natural language processing, and robotics. AI applications range from voice assistants to autonomous vehicles, and the field continues to evolve rapidly.
```

---

### 4️⃣ Practical Tips

- **Prompt design**  
  - Keep the instruction short and explicit.  
  - Example: `"Give a bullet‑point summary of the text below:"`.

- **Token limits**  
  - Models have a max context length (e.g., 4 k tokens for `gpt‑3.5‑turbo`).  
  - If your source text exceeds this, **split it into chunks**, summarize each chunk, then summarize the summaries.

- **Control length**  
  - Adjust `max_tokens` to cap the summary size.  
  - Use `temperature` ≈ 0.0–0.4 for concise, factual output.

- **Cost awareness**  
  - Summarization is cheap compared to generation, but longer inputs → higher cost.  
  - Use the **`text-davinci-003`** completion endpoint for a one‑shot summary if you prefer the older API style.

---

### 5️⃣ TL;DR (One‑Liner)

```python
summary = openai.ChatCompletion.create(
    model="gpt-3.5-turbo",
    messages=[{"role":"user","content":f"Summarize:\n\n{my_text}"}],
    temperature=0.3,
    max_tokens=150
).choices[0].message.content
```

That’s it—just send your text with a clear “summarize” instruction, and the API returns a neat, human‑readable summary!

Detective Mara Linton stared at the single, tarnished brass key lying on the kitchen table. It was the only clue the frantic homeowner had managed to bring from the scene—a modest, unassuming key with a faint engraving of a stylized owl.

The house was a mess of overturned furniture and shattered glass, but there was no sign of forced entry. The victim, a reclusive antiquarian named Mr. Whitaker, was found slumped over his desk, a single bullet wound in his chest. No weapon, no footprints, no witnesses—just the key.

Mara slipped the key into her pocket and began her investigation with the one thing it could unlock: its origin. She visited the local locksmith, an elderly man named Tomas who had been in the trade for half a century. He examined the key under a magnifying glass, his eyes narrowing.

“This isn’t a house key,” Tomas said, “It’s a drawer key—specifically for a safe. The owl engraving is the mark of Whitaker’s old university, St. Alden’s. They used that symbol for their secret society’s vaults.”

Mara thanked him and headed to St. Alden’s archives. The university’s records showed that the owl was indeed the emblem of the “Order of the Night,” a clandestine group of scholars who stored rare manuscripts in a hidden vault beneath the campus library. The vault’s lock required a brass key of this exact make.

She returned to Whitaker’s house and examined his desk. Behind a false panel, she found a narrow, dust‑caked tunnel leading down. At its end was a heavy iron door, its lock matching the key she held. Mara inserted the key, turned it, and the door groaned open.

Inside lay a small, climate‑controlled room filled with ancient codices, priceless artifacts, and a single, pristine notebook. The notebook’s pages were filled with meticulous notes about a recently discovered medieval manuscript—a work that could rewrite the history of the region. Whitaker had been on the verge of publishing his findings, a revelation that would have brought him fame and, more importantly, a fortune.

Mara’s eyes fell on a fresh ink blot on the last page—a hastily scrawled confession. It read: “I cannot let this fall into the wrong hands. If anyone discovers this, they will know I am the one who took it. I will meet you at the old pier at midnight. Bring the key.”

The ink was still wet. Mara realized the note had been written by the murderer, who had left the key as a taunt, hoping to mislead the investigation. But the clue was too precise; the murderer assumed the key would be the only thing anyone would notice.

Mara called in the local police, and together they set a trap at the pier. As the moon rose, a shadowy figure approached, clutching a satchel. When the detective stepped forward, the figure froze, then dropped the satchel—revealing a second, identical brass key.

It was Whitaker’s assistant, Dr. Felix Harrow, who had been helping catalog the collection. He had discovered the manuscript, realized its value, and plotted to steal it. He left the original key at the scene to create a false trail, hoping the police would focus on the university’s secret society. He brought a duplicate key to the pier, intending to retrieve the hidden vault’s contents later.

Mara’s single clue—a lone brass key—had led her straight to the truth. By tracing its origin, she uncovered a hidden vault, a secret society, and a desperate thief. The mystery was solved, the manuscript secured, and justice served—all because a detective learned to let a single clue speak louder than a thousand false leads.

followfly-1:
Below is a quick‑look timeline that captures the major milestones, people, and technologies that turned a handful of research‑grade computers into the global network we use today. Feel free to ask for deeper dives on any era or topic!

| Year | Milestone | Why it mattered |
|------|-----------|-----------------|
| **1950s‑1960s** | **Conceptual foundations** – J.C.R. Licklider’s “**Galactic Network**” vision (1962) and Paul Baran’s packet‑switching theory (1964). | Introduced the idea of a resilient, distributed network that could survive outages. |
| **1969** | **ARPANET** goes live (UCLA ↔ Stanford → U. Urbana). | First operational packet‑switched network; proved that geographically separated computers could talk. |
| **1971‑1972** | **Email** (Ray Tomlinson) and **File Transfer Protocol (FTP)** (Abhay Bhushan). | Added the first widely used applications, turning the network into a communication tool. |
| **1973** | **TCP/IP** (Vint Cerf & Bob Kahn) specification published. | Provided a universal, flexible protocol suite that could interconnect many different networks. |
| **1978** | **USENET** (Tom Truscott & Jim Ellis) – early distributed discussion system. | Precursor to modern forums and social media. |
| **1983** | **ARPANET adopts TCP/IP** (the “flag day”). | Unified the growing “network of networks” under a common language; the modern Internet is born. |
| **1985** | **Domain Name System (DNS)** (Paul Mockapetris). | Replaced numeric IP addresses with human‑readable names (e.g., `example.com`). |
| **1989** | **World Wide Web** proposal (Tim Berners‑Lee, CERN). | Introduced hypertext, URLs, and the HTTP protocol—making information easy to browse. |
| **1990‑1991** | First web server & browser (Berners‑Lee’s **CERN httpd** and **WorldWideWeb**). | Turned the Internet from a data‑exchange platform into a user‑friendly information space. |
| **1993** | **Mosaic** browser (Marc Andreessen & team). | Popularized graphical web browsing; sparked the “browser boom.” |
| **1994‑1995** | Commercialization – **Netscape Navigator**, **Yahoo!**, **Amazon**, **eBay**. | First wave of dot‑com startups; the Internet becomes a commercial marketplace. |
| **1996‑1998** | **Broadband** (DSL, cable) begins replacing dial‑up. | Faster, always‑on connections enable richer media (streaming, large downloads). |
| **1998** | **Google** founded. | Revolutionized web search, shaping how we discover information. |
| **2001‑2004** | **Web 2.0** – social platforms (Friendster, MySpace, Facebook 2004), **YouTube** (2005). | Shift from static pages to user‑generated content and interactive services. |
| **2007** | **iPhone** launch → **mobile Internet** explosion. | Smartphones make the Internet truly ubiquitous. |
| **2010‑2015** | **Cloud computing** (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) and **big data** analytics. | Services move from local servers to globally distributed data centers. |
| **2016‑present** | **Internet of Things (IoT)**, **5G**, **edge computing**, **AI‑driven services**. | Billions of devices, ultra‑low latency, and AI integration reshape everyday life. |

### Key Technological Layers

| Layer | Example | Role |
|-------|---------|------|
| **Physical** | Fiber optics, coax, satellite, 5G radio | Moves bits from point A to B. |
| **Link** | Ethernet, Wi‑Fi (IEEE 802.11) | Handles local delivery and error checking. |
| **Network** | **IP** (IPv4/IPv6) | Addresses each device on the global scale. |
| **Transport** | **TCP** (reliable) & **UDP** (fast, lossy) | Manages end‑to‑end data streams. |
| **Application** | HTTP/HTTPS, SMTP, DNS, FTP, WebSockets | Provides the services users see (web pages, email, video, etc.). |

### Why the Internet Works So Well

1. **Decentralization** – No single “owner”; many autonomous networks interconnect via standard protocols.  
2. **Scalability** – IPv6 expands the address space to 2³² × 2⁶⁴ ≈ 3.4 × 10³⁸ addresses, enough for every device imaginable.  
3. **Layered design** – Each layer can evolve independently (e.g., faster Wi‑Fi without changing HTTP).  
4. **Open standards** – Protocols are defined by bodies like IETF, ensuring interoperability across vendors and countries.

### Suggested Next Steps

| Goal | Resources |
|------|-----------|
| **Deep dive into early ARPANET** | *“Where Wizards Stay Up Late”* by Katie Hafner & Matthew Lyon (book). |
| **Learn TCP/IP fundamentals** | **RFC 791** (IP) and **RFC 793** (TCP) – original specifications (readable summaries on [ietf.org](https://www.ietf.org/)). |
| **Explore the birth of the Web** | Tim Berners‑Lee’s original proposal (1990) – available on CERN’s website. |
| **Understand modern Internet governance** | Look at the roles of **IANA**, **ICANN**, and regional internet registries (RIRs). |
| **Hands‑on practice** | Set up a small home lab with **VirtualBox** or **Docker** and run a simple web server (e.g., `python -m http.server`). |

---

**Quick recap:** The Internet started as a government‑funded research project (ARPANET) in the late 1960s, adopted the robust TCP/IP suite in the early 1980s, gained a user‑friendly interface with the World Wide Web in 1990, and has since exploded into a global, mobile, cloud‑driven ecosystem that powers everything from social media to IoT devices.

Let me know which era or technology you’d like to explore further, or if you’d like recommendations for books, documentaries, or hands‑on projects!

Once upon a time, in a quiet valley tucked between whispering hills, I lived as a modest apprentice to my father, a woodcutter. I spent my days hauling timber and my evenings dreaming of distant kingdoms, never suspecting that the greatest adventure would begin in the hearth of our own cottage.

One crisp autumn morning, a traveling minstrel arrived, his lute singing of far‑off feasts and golden banquets. He knocked upon our door, his eyes bright with hunger. “Good folk,” he cried, “I have journeyed far and my stomach growls louder than the dragon’s roar. Might you spare a morsel?”

My father, weary from the forest, could offer only a thin slice of bread. I, eager to please, fetched a pot and a handful of herbs from the garden. As the minstrel watched, I clumsily tossed the herbs into the pot, added a splash of water, and whispered a hopeful prayer.

“Do not fear, little one,” the minstrel said, smiling. “Even the smallest flame can warm a kingdom.”

When the broth simmered, a fragrant steam rose, filling the cottage with a scent sweeter than any wildflower. The minstell’s eyes widened. “What magic is this?” he asked.

I blushed and answered, “I do not know, sir. I merely followed the rhythm of the fire.”

He tasted the broth, and his face lit like sunrise. “By the stars! You have a gift, dear child. This broth could heal a wounded knight and delight a queen.”

Word of my humble soup spread through the village like a golden thread. The baker, the miller, even the stern mayor came to taste my creations. Each dish I prepared seemed to sing, to tell a story of the forest, the river, and the wind.

One night, as I stirred a pot of stew, the old crone who lived at the edge of the woods entered. “Child,” she croaked, “the kingdom beyond the hills seeks a chef whose heart is pure. Will you go?”

I hesitated, but the fire within me burned brighter than any fear. “I will,” I declared, “for I have learned that a humble pot can hold the power of a kingdom.”

And so I set forth, my ladle as my sword, my recipes as my spells. The kingdom feasted, and peace blossomed, for the people were nourished in body and spirit.

**Moral:** True talent, once discovered, can turn the simplest hearth into a beacon of hope; nurture it, and you may feed not only bellies, but also hearts.

metro-mapper-1:
Below is a **concise, prioritized list of the Google Maps Platform APIs that are directly useful for building an application that shows **multiple maps, places markers on them, and draws routes** (directions) between points.  
Anything not listed can generally be ignored for this specific use‑case.

| # | API | Why it’s needed for “multiple maps + markers + routes” |
|---|-----|------------------------------------------------------|
| **1** | **Maps JavaScript API** | Core library for rendering interactive maps in a web page, adding multiple map instances, customizing controls, and placing markers, polylines, polygons, and other overlays. |
| **2** | **Directions API** | Generates turn‑by‑turn routes (driving, walking, bicycling, transit) and returns the polyline data you can draw on a map. |
| **3** | **Places API (Places Library for JavaScript)** | Provides place search, autocomplete, and place details so you can let users pick locations and automatically add markers with rich info (name, address, photos, etc.). |
| **4** | **Geocoding API** | Converts user‑entered addresses or place names to latitude/longitude coordinates (needed before you can place a marker or request a route). |
| **5** | **Maps Static API** *(optional)* | If you need a quick, non‑interactive snapshot of a map (e.g., for email or PDF export) with markers and paths baked into the image. |
| **6** | **Maps SDK for Android** / **Maps SDK for iOS** *(if you’re building native mobile apps)* | Native equivalents of the JavaScript API for Android or iOS, supporting multiple map fragments, markers, and directions overlays. |
| **7** | **Roads API** *(optional but handy)* | “Snap‑to‑road” functionality to align raw GPS points to the nearest road, useful when you want routes that follow the road network precisely. |
| **8** | **Distance Matrix API** *(optional)* | If you need travel time / distance calculations between many origin‑destination pairs (e.g., for optimizing multiple routes). |
| **9** | **Elevation API** *(rarely needed for basic routing)* | Provides elevation data for points along a route; useful only for specialized visualizations (e.g., elevation profiles). |
| **10** | **Maps Embed API** *(optional)* | Quick way to embed a pre‑configured map with markers or directions via an `<iframe>` – useful for simple read‑only views. |

### Quick “starter” stack
If you’re just getting started, the **minimum** set you’ll need is:

1. **Maps JavaScript API** – render the map(s) and add markers/polylines.  
2. **Directions API** – fetch route geometry.  
3. **Geocoding API** (or the Places Library) – turn user‑entered addresses into coordinates.

All three can be called from the same client‑side JavaScript code (or via a lightweight backend proxy if you need to hide your API key).

### How they fit together (high‑level flow)

1. **User selects/enters locations** →  
   - Use **Places Autocomplete** (from the Places Library) or **Geocoding API** to get lat/lng.  
2. **Create a map instance** (or multiple instances) with **Maps JavaScript API**.  
3. **Add a `Marker`** for each location on the appropriate map.  
4. **Request a route** from **Directions API** (pass origin, destination, and any waypoints).  
5. **Render the returned polyline** on the map using the `Polyline` class.  
6. (Optional) Use **Roads API** to snap raw GPS points to the road network before drawing.  
7. (Optional) Use **Distance Matrix API** if you need travel‑time estimates for many point pairs.  

### What you can safely ignore for this use‑case
- **Maps Tile API** – low‑level tile serving, not needed for standard map rendering.  
- **Street View API** – only if you want embedded 360° imagery.  
- **Geolocation API** – only for automatically detecting the user’s current location (optional).  
- **Maps SDK for Unity / WebGL** – not relevant unless you’re building a game or Unity app.  
- **Maps Data API** – for editing custom map data layers (overkill for simple markers/routes).  

---

**Next steps:**  
1. Enable the **Maps JavaScript API**, **Directions API**, and **Geocoding API** (or Places Library) in the Google Cloud Console.  
2. Obtain an API key with the appropriate restrictions (HTTP referrer for web, package name + SHA‑1 for mobile).  
3. Follow the quick‑start guides for each API to get a basic map with a marker, then add a directions request and render the polyline.  

Feel free to ask for sample code snippets or deeper guidance on any of the listed APIs!
